lead: I built most of these with friends, and several at hackathons. Each entry says what the project does and which part I built.

projects.name: Morro

figure.alt: Four maps comparing the change in precipitation under four simulated cloud-seeding methods
figure.caption: Precipitation change 126 hours after seeding, for four methods, over a Middle East drought.

paras: Morro is a simulator for the people who would have to decide on a weather intervention before a disaster arrives. It forecasts ten days ahead with two AI weather models, GraphCast and NVIDIA Earth2Studio, and flags droughts and forming cyclones. Then it reruns the forecast under each of four cloud-seeding methods and ranks them by how much they help.

I built the pipeline that applies each seeding method. It turns a method into a physics-calibrated change to the model’s starting atmosphere, and that change carries through the ten-day forecast. I also trained the Random Forest classifiers that detect drought severity and cyclone formation from ERA5 reanalysis data. I built Morro with Tej Kosaraju and Kieran P.
projects.note: We built this in a weekend. A change in a forecast is not evidence that seeding would work in the real atmosphere.

projects.name: OceanOps

figure.alt: OceanOps mission control, with plume controls, a heat map off the California coast and modeled ocean chemistry
figure.caption: Mission control in the public demo, which runs on bundled ocean conditions.

paras: OceanOps is a shipboard planning tool for ocean alkalinity enhancement, which removes carbon by adding alkaline material to seawater so it absorbs more carbon dioxide. You change a vessel’s speed, discharge rate or feedstock and see how the modeled plume and the water chemistry respond. You can then plan fleet routes around marine traffic and protected areas.

I built fleet telemetry over NATS with an HTTP fallback, the AI analysis panel, the map overlays and the simulation flow, and I fixed route rendering. I worked on it with Akshat Choudhari and Yashmit Bhaverisetti.
projects.note: This is a planning prototype. The demo’s chemistry thresholds, plume and carbon estimates are illustrative.

projects.name: CourseLens
projects.meta: Data Science Teaching and Learning Lab · paper at SIGCSE TS 2027

figure.title: The Edit Is Not the End
figure.subtitle: CourseLens for Reviewing AI-Proposed Course Updates
figure.authors: Andrew Yang, Susana Haing, Thaarak Sriram, Chengyun Xu, Zhiqing Wang, Sam Lau
figure.caption: CourseLens accompanies this paper.

paras: Instructors have started asking AI coding agents to update whole courses. The agent edits many files, and someone has to check them before students see them. CourseLens lays the proposed edits out in the order the course is taught and shows each one in the rendered lecture or assignment. It also reads the agent’s activity log to mark which files the agent changed, which it only checked, and which it never opened.
I’m one of the paper’s six authors and part of the team that built the tool, with Andrew Yang, Susana Haing, Chengyun Xu, Zhiqing Wang and Sam Lau.
projects.note: CourseLens never edits course files. The instructor still decides whether each change is correct.

projects.name: Triton Hub
projects.meta: A student dashboard for UC San Diego

figure.alt: Triton Hub dashboard showing sample coursework, email and deadlines
figure.caption: The public demo uses fictional courses and messages.

paras: Deadlines at UC San Diego arrive in several places at once. Triton Hub pulls Canvas assignments, grades and announcements, academic email and a personal calendar into one feed.

I wired live Canvas data into the assignment and announcement views, and built calendar events and completion tracking on Supabase. I worked on it with Rayirth Dinesh, Siddharth Maddikayala and shrivassudharsan1.

projects.name: Solar Registry Screening

head: Rank
Example plant
Capacity
Score
figure.caption: The bundled demo starts with five fictional installations. Three qualify, and eleven rules score each one out of 100.

paras: This pipeline takes a solar registry export, validates the records, and filters them down to the installations that qualify. It ranks what is left with explicit rules, so every score comes with the points and reasons behind it.

I designed it to run the cheapest step first. The rule-based ranking runs offline on registry fields alone, and only the shortlist goes on to geospatial matching or optional model-assisted scoring. When a match is ambiguous, the pipeline leaves it unresolved.
projects.note: The public repository contains only synthetic examples. The scores show how the screening method works and are not investment advice.

projects.name: Arnold

figure.alt: Arnold showing a meal draft with portions and nutrition estimates, ready for review
figure.caption: Arnold shows a meal entry for review before saving it.

paras: Arnold is a fitness journal you talk to. You describe a meal or a workout in plain English, check what Arnold understood, then save it.

I added plain-English meal and workout logging, USDA food lookup, exercise search and the voice flow to our hackathon prototype. For the public version I rebuilt logging so it previews portions and nutrients before it saves anything. Shrish Premkrishna, Kenny, Jello and I built the original.

projects.name: Wendy

figure.alt: Wendy’s planning chat with prompts for venue search, inquiry drafts and guest RSVPs
figure.caption: The demo uses fictional venues and never sends anything.

paras: Wendy keeps venue search, guest lists and planning conversations in one place. You set a budget and a guest count and shortlist venues, and Wendy drafts an inquiry from details already in the conversation.

I built the venue-search tool, connected it to chat, and wrote the reservation-request flow that collects event details and drafts the inquiry. I worked on it with Shrish Premkrishna, Aryaman Gandhi and Kenny.
